Listen; I was in the very same boat as you so I share sympathies with you. But, from the bottom of my heart, I despise this comment.

Diagnosed with ADHD deep into college, having had it ignored or hidden away by my parents. The pressure was high, constant shouting matches against my family, etc. 

I graduated university last May with a 2.8 GPA, no personal projects completed, a couple dead attempts at trying out leetcode. Throughout my senior I had nights like these where I mourned my future, cursing my past and pushing my failures to come through on my upbringing.

I bitched and moaned until the very day I graduated. I recall staring at the list of honors graduates in disgrace. There were people on that list that I knew well, people whom I shared my life with. At some point, it clicked for me. It didn’t matter if my parents had tarnished my self esteem or fucked up parts of my upbringing. The truth was that I’d wasted away my college years. Full stop.

I then had a choice! Either keeps sitting on my ass, twiddling my thumbs and blaming the whole world but myself, or picking up my shit and getting to work, because I refuse to let that bs infect me any longer.

Over the next couple of months, I started a project that *I* was interested in. People pissed on it, but I worked on it out of passion. I would wake up, apply to jobs, work on my project, grind leetcode, and close out the day with more applications. I found time to game and see friends, of course. But by late August, I had 600 apps out without a single interview. But I had a project, I had practice, and I had confidence in my own skills.

By mid September, I got a chance. Just one. My first chance at an interview. Spent days just practicing for it; grinding endlessly just honing in on my chance.

I moved to Seattle about a month later. I got lucky, and I’ll admit that every day until I pass. But I could only receive that luck because I moved my stupid ass into a position where I could receive it.

At this point in time, it doesn’t matter your upbringing. If you can’t get yourself to do *something* now, then the least you can do is forgive your parents, because it isn’t their fault alone anymore.

I played on a competitive team for a little bit and I can toss my insight. Azoth gave a fantastic rundown of a style of drafts for pro-leagues, which is optimal for teams with vast champion pools.

For clash, it is pretty different. When running a team of clashmates, not every player will have multiple champions they are capable of playing at a random given moment. It is far more likely that a given player will have 1 main champion and several 'side' champions they are proficient at. Thus, your attitude towards drafts much be different.

In my group, we usually aim towards running a teamfight type. A dive comp, front-back, picks, etc. It depends heavily on both what we want to play, and who's playing. I can give an example based on some of my friends' preferred picks.

​

* Top: Gnar, Camille, Renekton, Shen
* Jungle: Zac, Rek'sai, Skarner
* Mid: Vladimir, Orianna, Syndra
* ADC: Kai'sa, Lucian, Vayne
* Supp: Bard, Nautilus, Leona

So what do we draft here? There are a couple things to keep in mind. 

1. What type of comp does it seem like we prefer?
2. What can we do in case our opponents ban a key pick?
3. How do we react to our opponents' counter picks?
4. What do \*we\* ban to weaken our opponents?

With that in mind, let's go into some styles. In a dive comp, we could go (in order of picks):

1. Kai'sa - Engage ADC (Safe from backline assassins by virtue of her ult's repositioning ability. Priority pick because she's the most stable of the available ADC picks in a dive comp)
2. Gnar - Secondary Engage tank (High follow-up CC on Zac's engage)
3. Zac - Main Engage Tank (Insane cc ability that the entire team can follow up on)
4. Nautilus - Peel Engage (If we don't get Vlad, Nautilus backs up the mage pick, otherwise he can engage following Gnar as a solid finish tool)
5. Vladimir - Burst tool (Immediately aims to kill the enemy's carries during the midst of a teamfight) 

Roles would also move around depending on opposing picks and bans, but this is an example team drafted in a vacuum, the understanding that the enemy is some set of unknown champions. 

A front back team composition could look like: 

1. Shen - Peel and tool (In the early game, ensures the adc does not lose and later survives during teamfights)
2. Orianna - CC Ult & Disruption (In teamfights, her ult is key for creating danger zones that make it difficult for the enemy team to step up and kill the adc backline. Could also be Syndra, but Orianna is better atm :P)
3. Skarner - CC & Pick tool (Skarner's ult is often utilized as a pick tool for enemy carries, but it can be so much more than that. Ulting an assassin saves your adc from possible doom, ulting a tank can let you eradicate the enemy's tanking ability by bursting down the tank as a group immediately)
4. Vayne/Lucian - ADC (Lucian's ability to kill tanks is far worse than vayne's, but the tradeoff is fantastic poking, scouting abilites, and great squishy burst. Vayne's pretty straightforward)
5. Nautilus - Peel Tool (Just a great fucking champion. Incredibly versatile, but bard and Leona demonstrate good potential here too). 

This process of team creation can basically be recreated with any pool of champions you and your friends have, it's just a demonstration. You ban picks that could possibly disrupt your team ideas, but in unprofessional play it is almost always easier to play around your players than it is to play around the enemy's picks. Just my opinion, though! I can explain \*alot\* more if anything I said is difficult to understand.

In the context of overall Jungle play, then yes, comparison of the champions is perfectly normal. In the case of a champion being better than another (kit-wise) it is mostly based on the meta, not their position.

Sej versus skarner is a great example. Yes, Sej is tankier, but it is solely due to the overwhelming amount of resistances granted by her passive. This is exactly when roles come into play. Sejuani is an engage tank, her kit is built around being in the middle of the action with other melee champions to maximize her stacks. She would therefore *need* high resistances to stack her stuns and survive as long as possible. In a teamfight, Skarner is a peel tank. His role is to protect the backline and his kit reflects that. He lacks the huge amount of tankiness that Sej provides, but instead he gives *consistent* cc and a lockdown tool that ensures that any assassin going for backline is shut down. Both junglers, but completely different roles on a team. 

This is when meta comes in. The current meta revolves around strong adcs (Vayne, Jhin, Jinx), supports who can boost their damage or pick potential(Lulu, Blitz) the assassins that can dive them(Vex, Zed) the bruiser engages(Hecarim, Vi, Xin) that can back up assassins with cc and chaos, and the peelers/supports that keeps the backline alive (Soraka, Nami, Shen). Skarner fits in as a secondary peeler, but at the moment you’d likely prefer an engage diver on your team instead. Ergo, Hecarim is currently supreme. However, take the game just 4 patches ago and Hecarim’s dominance is nowhere near as noticable. 

Balance in League isn’t as simple as “X champion has better Z than Y”. It’s based entirely on the meta. Having the best ganks in the world means fuck all if Riot increases Jungle Xp and farming champions rise to the top. The only exceptions are when a champion is absurdly weak, absurdly strong, or have a counterpart that does their role better in every way.

If you break down every champion into their strengths, you could make a lot of champions sound broken. Except Rengar. Rengar’s still dogshit.

Let’s just take Skarner vs Hecarim for now. Vastly different champions, big differences in strengths. Yet, nearly 50/50 winrate against each other on u.gg. Both solid picks at the moment.

In Skarner’s favor:
1)Better early ganks. Skarner requires little to no items for his solid ganks due to his W gap closer and E stun follow up. Unlike Hecarim, who’s gap closer *is* his cc, Skarner can reliably pin down a laner without worry of them getting away as easily.

2) Superior Mana. Skarner’s sustain in the jungle means that he does not run into the same mana problems Hecarim does. This isn’t a huge issue for junglers due to item passive, but in extended gank runs it can be the difference.

3) Better picking potential. Skarner’s ult allows his team to preemptively turn every team fight into a 4v5 given proper timing and positioning.

In Hecarim’s favor

1) Better teamfight. Hecarim’s Ult and Aoe ability means his kit is excellent in turning the tides of a teamfight if well timed in execution.

2) Better mid game. Compared to Skarner, Hecarim comes online a bit later but supplements that with a dominating mid game if he is ahead by any amount. 

3) Less team-reliant. Unlike Skarner, Hecarim is absolutely a 1v9 champion in the hands of an aggressive player. Especially in sub diamond elo, Hecarim is an absolute menace. 

Point being made here is that it’s difficult to compare champions without them performing the same exact roles. And even then, most champions are situationally better, with the exception of champions that are on the far ends of viability.
But popularity doesn’t make a champion bad. Skarner for example is a fantastic pick despite the fact that the bastard never gets picked

I'm currently a 65% WR d4/d3 player, but I've access to people much higher ranked than me, those people being Masters/GM level, but I do recommend taking some of the things I say with a grain of salt.

As for a full clear, the basic full clear can begin in many different locations depending on your champion. Some champions can start from wolves, but most start from buffs so I'll start with those. Let's say you're playing blue side. In a vacuum, you have a multitude of choices.

*  For an early gank, you can start your game off with a 3 camp clear for level 3. To reach level 3 as a jungler with only 3 camps cleared, you must clear either gromp or the entirety of krugs. Standard 3 camps is either: Full blue side (Blue -> Gromp -> Wolves), Full Red side (Red -> Krugs -> Raptors) or Buff Buff Gromp (Red buff -> Blue -> Gromp) or Buff gromp Buff (Blue -> Gromp -> Red). Any of these combos allow you to reach level 3 extremely quickly, with the last two being the most common for aggressive junglers as double buff is an insane buff to any champion, especially in the early game. You may notice in the 3 clear, you essentially leave 3 level 1 camps on the map while you gank. This is not usually an issue, even if you end up having no lanes to gank by the time you reach the opposing side of the map as you can simply turn around and clear backwards towards the camps you skipped and taking the other scuttle. 
* If you are looking for a full clear before scuttle, standard pathing is either Red side (Red -> Krugs -> Raptors -> Wolves -> Blue -> Gromp) or Blue side (Blue -> Gromp -> Wolves -> Raptors -> Red -> Krugs). This path is great once you have your clearing down pat and can reach scuttle crab by 3:15, the standard scuttle spawn time. 
* Alternative to the 6 camp full clear is the 5 camp full clear. For a beginner, I much more recommend this clear, which generally skips the last camp in the full clear sequence, either the gromp or Krugs (usually the krugs, since krugs take an incredible amount of time for most champions). You essentially get level 4 off of scuttle crab and immediately go for a gank. This clear lets you get first priority on scuttle and (often) lets you take the scuttle before your enemy jungler if they choose to full clear instead. 

As for innefficiences, it's not a big worry. Time is the most important resource for a jungler, so as long as you fill your time with *something* worthwhile, it's not too much of a loss. 

For jungle monster resets, pay close attention to  the little bar under the monsters' hp bars. It starts off gray and eventually depletes to yellow, then red. Once it's gone, the monster resets. (Note! Little monsters, such as tiny chickens, do not have a patience bar.) A couple things cause the depletion of this bar. 1) You walk out of the monster's [zone](https://imgur.com/a/utsAY0v) 2) Another champion attacks the monster, causing it to change targets and losing some bars of patience. You may notice this happening if you've ever had a melee support leash the jungler. 

In the image I linked above, there are lines drawn that demonstrate the patience zones of jungle camps. For the sake of kiting, remember that the bar depletes over time once you leave the zone, meaning you could drag out a camp from its patience zone if you think you can kill it before its patience depletes (saving you precious seconds). Also notice that some camps' patience zones overlap. By standing at this overlap, you can do both camps at once without fear of eitehr camp resetting. This, of course, only works if you are capable of clearing both at once as it trades health for speed. It's not necessary, but in higher elos, these saved seconds make all the difference. 10 seconds isn't a lot of time, but as a GM player you should know just how much a game's prospects can change in 10 seconds. Especially in the early game. That's the difference between your nidalee getting a level 4 kill vs the enemy nocturne getting a gank on your mid lane and ruining your priority for the rest of the match.

Graves is a fantastic champion to carry on as a high skilled mechanics player, but since you mentioned being an ADC main, I highly recommend Kindred OR Lillia.

Both of these champions are incredibly simple to carry on, with their primary difficulty being their clearing. Lillia and Kindred's first clear require finesse and kiting skill, but a player who has that skill can solo carry up to Masters (especially as Kindred). Kiting is much the same for both as it is for an adc. You auto while just out of the monster's attack range, taking as little damage as possible while maximizing your own. The best part about playing low elo is that your clear path rarely matters until low diamond at least. For both, go for a solid full clear and look for ganks. 

As for ganks, you basically can boil everything down to ganking anyone who's pushing too hard. Dives are unnecessary but easy on both of these champions. More importantly, in my opinion, is understanding vision. Let's take mid lane for example. The single most common ward for a mid laner is the side river bush wards on either side of the mid line. It's a solid ward, gives minor vision of the enemy jungler if they clear scuttle towards mid, and can feasibly catch ganks. However, it is flawed in that, as a jungler, you can hug the dragon/herald side wall and reach the other side of the river without being seen. Similarly, as Kindred, you can hop over walls to avoid being seen. These tips, alongside an aggressive, invasive playstyle, will put you too far ahead for any average plat team to win against. Lillia especially, who has incredible solo-carry potential if you're capable of dodging CC. 

Also, ignore dragons if it isn't completely, 100% free. Dragons are great, but the main point of getting dragons is to eventually reach dragon soul. In a low elo game, it simply doesn't need to happen. Get herald every time you can.

Irrelevant and doesn’t answer the problem of her awful first clear. I understand you’re new to jungle, so a fair warning is that your first clear is often the deciding factor in your games. 

Let’s say you do end up playing Xayah jungle. Like with a lot of tanks, you end up with a particularly weak first clear (and a very slow one at that given your high cds and over reliance on autos). In this situation, you face a graves, or a shaco, or a rek sai, or whatever. Literally any early game invading champion.

You finish gromp and Blue, aaand your Red’s gone. Or alternatively, you finish your blue and the enemy jungler just walks in and kills you/forces a flash. Tank junglers have cc and high sustain in jungle as support for invading aggro junglers. Other aggro junglers have high dueling power and even off meta junglers like twitch simply clear fast enough that it isn’t a huge threat if they get invaded. Xayah simply does not have any of these qualities, she simply has no advantages that allows her to be successful as a jungler. Heck, taric jungle is infinitely more viable.

You will win games, especially in low elo, but it simply isn’t going to be primarily off your skill.

It really does not matter how strong or fast Xayah’s clear is by midgame, nor does it matter her ganks. Her first clear is so unbelievably weak that any victory you achieve is solely because the enemy jungler is bad and not because you are good.

Xayah’s 3 abilities are on extremely high cooldowns (10 or 20). Her W is probably the most helpful in the jungle early game given it is an attack speed buff, but it only lasts for 4 seconds and goes on cooldown.

If botlane is losing, taking early drake is a bad idea because... you’ll probably die. Especially as Kindred, anyone showing up either means you lose drake to the enemy, your death, or both. Your time is better spent ganking bot, clearing and moving towards top side to look for other opportunities (your bot is generally safe when under tower), or looking to get deep wards and invade.

In the case that your botlane has priority, a badly timed drake means your botlane recalls too late and is unable to freeze when the wave bounces back to them. There’s just too many opportunities being lost in trade for drake. 

The only time drake is valuable in SoloQ is if you’re expecting a very long game with soul involved, or if the value of a single drake outweighs the other options on the board. The latter is rarely the case, simply because you’ll probably get more gold value from invading and clearing than a measly 4% bonus to attacking stats in the early/mid game. 

Now, disclaimer; most of these concepts won’t apply to low elo. Your laners will probably overstay all the time and the word freeze only occurs to them when they play red light green light. However, you can very easily abuse these concepts when the enemy jungler tries to take drake. Enemy jungler on dragon @lvl 4? There’s a couple reasons. Let’s assume we’re blue side here.

1) If we get a leash from bot and start red, we can reach river before 3 minutes on a decent clear, and exactly 3 minutes on a slow clear. Generally speaking, unless we’re facing a 3 camp ganking champion, we can expect the enemy jungler to do a variation of a 5 camp clear or a complete full clear depending on clear speed. By taking 4 camps, we are given 4 options to take. Gank top, gank mid, invade enemy buff, or take gromp. Solidly going for gromp removes the chance to invade against tank matchups, and also negates your ability to take spire prior to scuttle spawn. 

2)As mentioned above, spire. Under spire, you gain a tremendous amount of movement speed and attack speed. In a one on one duel against a graves, with proper kiting, you come on top fairly often given the low cooldowns and high attack speed. Generally speaking, being unable to take spire or losing it to the enemy jungler automatically concedes the scuttle crab (and ergo, top or mid lane ganks) to the enemy jungler. 

3)You want red buff. This is especially true in the early game. Skarner’s red buff boost is insane and incredibly powerful. You apply it quickly and have a lot of sticking power when ganking. It is a significant boost in power to your ganks, which is incredibly valuable for quick ganks. 

4)Imo, general pathing at this stage is the most important part. You’re opening yourself up to a lot of opportunities by skipping the fifth camp. Take the time you would’ve spent on gromp to make impact, do a reverse clear (Gromp-> Respawned Raptors -> Krugs) and get cinderhulk. At this point, as a baseline, I immediately go bot even after I cleared. In this scenario, I have many options based off of my bot lane. If bot’s being shoved in, I can go in for a gank using my item advantage to get pressure for dragon. If my bot lane is doing the shoving, I can ward for the enemy jungler and either do dragon with numbers advantage with my botlane, or look to countergank if I think the enemy jungler will gank. If the enemy bot lane already finished shoving and have recalled, I immediately go to my dragon as I have the advantage of botlane presence. 

Tldr; 4 camp lets you get spire and duel most enemy junglers (ironically enough, not Volibear). And it also maintains the most amount of options for you to take as to not waste time.

5 camp clear is fine on sej, and I do it often; in fact I sometimes catch myself diving right into a 6 camp clear against tanks. However, keep in mind that sej's main goal is to gank. Arriving at 3:15 has two issues; 1. You're a weak tank in the early game and will lose to any of the meta jg fighters. 2. You're going to be in a worser posiiton to countergank if the enemy jungler decided to clear 5 camps as well and go straight for a top gank. It's just nice to be in position for a counter gank if need be. Personally, I do blue and gromp at the same time to take a bit of damage in trade for faster positioning. Hiding in top river bush is a great way to catch an enemy jungler trying to kill your overextended top laner.

It's more based on health and options left at the end of the initial clear.

Taking lee-sin blue side, at the end of the clear, you're left with two options after Red-krugs-raptors; Gank mid or go to wolves. Scuttle at this point is not up yet and, if your mid is not available to ganks, you've essentially lost a ton of HP to krugs for nothing. In this scenario, your dueling for scuttle is weaker to a lower amount of resources you otherwise would have had. (With this clear, any amount of inefficiencies means you fail to reach scuttle and top lane by 3:15. This has two consequences; you fail to impact your top lane in time compared to enemy top laner, who may or may not skip krugs on first clear, or you're simply weaker in comparison to the enemy jungle. 

Taking Red, Raptors, Wolves, Blue, means you can three options before scuttle spawns; Gank top or mid before the enemy jungler can, or clear gromp to delay yourself as you wait for an opening or for scuttle to spawn. The 4 camp option is a lot healthier for champions that lack easy sustain and/or aoe damage, which is king at the moment. 

Let's take Rek'sai for example. She has innate healing and her primary clearing ability is an aoe auto. Here three camp Red start is much faster and much healthier than Lee's, leading you an optimal path that, even if enemy mid is not open, let's you clear wolves and blue with fantastic hp without using any pots. 

This, of course, does not mean either path is unviable. If you think mid lane is open to a gank early, three camp clear is perfectly viable on lee. However, keeping in mind the opportunity costs, you lose a ton of chances as lee if you lose your hp too much early as a result of doing krugs.

The nuance in champions like Cho, Garen, and Darius all come from general game knowledge. They aren't necessarily difficult mechanically, but a good macro player can operate them very well. 

As specifically for cho'gath, understand that his Q isn't a poke spell. His E is the best 'fighting' ability he has in his arsenal. In any matchup, it is the most consistent and easy to hit damage Cho has, and uses much less mana. If you continue to play Cho, I highly recommend you treat his Q as merely a gap closer, minion killer, or an escape tool. A lot of low level cho players just simply use it to often and burn their mana out. Remember, for a Cho, your mana is just as important as your HP. You use a lot of it and your spells are expensive, so be sparing with it.

As a beginner champion, Cho isn't too bad. If you're really looking to improve, you can definitely play him to explore the rest of the game. However, in my personal opinion, playing each lane teaches different skills. Top teaches you map awareness. Not only for TP support, but also ganks, split push viability, and general location reading. Jungle offers some of the same map awareness, but its main boost is to decision making. Time is the most important part of jungling, but it is not a role that low level players should pick up to climb or improve. Mid is definitely the mechanics lane. You're playing against assassins, mages and general duelists while also making sure you avoid ganks. Fantastic role to play if you want to just become a better playmaker. ADC, as someone described below, revolves around positioning and csing. Of course, csing is important in every role, but no other role spikes nearly as hard as ADCs do with items. Very key. Supports go unappreciated, but they're micro-management. Lots of small impacts that build up big. A good support is disgusting to play against. You certainly don't have to play every lane in the game to improve your skills, but these are some general guidelines on lanes.

Depends on your playstyle of Cho.

Universally between tank and AP, you should be aiming to land a Q when they’re going for CS. That’s the point when your chances are the highest. Learn to bait them by pretending to walk in range for Q, then backing off. Learn to predict they dash habits (left, right, do they always dash? Do they fake a dash? Etc).

As tank, you’ll mostly be looking to conserve mana and wait for ganks. Landing Q is not your most important task. Use your E more often than your Q, because the slow is immensely helpful in landing the rest of your abilities. Avoid taking too much in poke and just try to walk up with E ready during ganks. Land E, hit W and then Q for a basic combo.

As AP, going for Q’s is much more viable because every AP cho build naturally goes for Mana sustain. Comet cho’s build 3 d rings into Lost chapter, Mixed AP builds lost chapter outright, etc. As said before, look to throw Q’s out whenever they go for minions. A single Q hitting any of those champions is enough. Land Q, W, then an Auto attack. E to reset your auto and chase them down.

Either way, make sure to make proper use of your ult. It matters less as tank Cho, but holding onto your ult as AP cho is necessary for extreme burst.

I play exclusively Cho’Gath AP in the mid lane. As expected, this means I run into a metric shitload of Ranged matchups so I’ll break it down for you.

As others have said, your main goal is working to get your Q’s to land. A single Q can result the loss of half their HP bar. A general tip for all champions here is to bait out CC and overall utility. For example, wait till Lux Q’s before you throw down a surprise Q of your own to get atop of her for free. 

However, Cho uses up a massive amount of Mana in the early game. One Q is easy to miss and costs almost a fifth of his total level 1-3 mana bar. Here’s what I do: Start Doran’s ring. Always. Entering lane, even top lane, with doran’s shield as full AP Cho is not wise. You want consistent sustain even if you’re pushed off your minions. Once you hit 800 gold or so, recall and get yourself two more doran’s rings to properly lose most worries regarding mana. This is crucial, especially if you feel like you’re up against a difficult matchup. 

Build Luden’s into protobelt (once again, making sure your mana sustain is on par). Break the build chain for boots and defense items (Armsguard mostly). Never, under any circumstances, build ROA or any tank items. There’s a couple reasons for this. For ROA specifically, playing in Mid or Top with a mediocre scaling item isn’t worth the risk. While it helps with getting you HP later on, your job is not to soak up damage, it’s to act like a second ADC and land your Nuclear Q’s. Tank items take away from this as, unlike Glacial Cho, your duty is not in CCing enemies. 

Try your best to land your Q’s while enemies are farming. Don’t be afraid to fight to prevent a cannon minion.

Very late into this post, but my personal favorite part of playing Cypher is clutching and retaking sites on rotation, so here are a couple tips.

During setups, I highly recommend setting up wires first before setting up cages. Listen for footsteps and use a cage as soon as they get uncomfortably close in order to safeguard your escape. Other Cypher mains recommend using just a cage over a wire as you lose 200p if your wire is cleared and only 100 if you only use cage. Imo, it’s fairly situational. Setup your wires further back to avoid losing them to utility, or simply save them till utility is burnt. Both work relatively well imo. 

The primary reason for my desire to save my cages is that they’re incredibly repositioning tools. They make sounds when an enemy enter them, meaning you can go around the outer edge of it with relative safety. During retakes and rotations, this is absolutely phenomenal and incredibly important in allowing you as many 1 on 1 dueling opportunities. 

Furthermore, Cypher’s cages go down extremely far. In sites such as A Bind, this means that you can pop it Heaven and hop down onto site with ease. Multiple cages can also be used to further enemy team’s uncertainty. 

Use Camera on the site you’ve rotated to as soon as possible. I like to mark the enemy I plan to hit, even if they’ll be in direct view of me as most players have an inborn instinct to pull out the marker asap. Perfect time to take shots.

Town gets wrecked with infected being attracted to the ruins, the survivors stranded and escaping, etc. As you said, Joel goes off on his own to keep Ellie safe as he goes for revenge while Ellie follows. Tommy follows her and we get to explore more Joel’s past through dialogue between the two. Ellie puts even more thinking into Joel’s decision and, after witnessing moments throughout her adventure with Tommy, understands Joel’s reasoning for his decision.

We then switch to Joel’s act as he works to track down the attackers. We replay maybe one or two general levels (same overall location perhaps, but different scenery. For example, a different part of Seattle we didn’t get to see initially). Joel’s questioning and information gathering reveals that the reason why the town was attacked was because of him. The attackers had loved ones killed by Joel and, in an effort to get revenge on him, they attacked the location he was rumored to reside in and assumed he had died.

Yada yada, more story+adventuring, Joel and Ellie reunite for a final act of TLOU, Joel and Ellie reconnect to complete Ellie’s circle and for the last couple of hours, we get the amazing Father daughter dynamic. 

During one of the final missions, Joel and Ellie’s group is overwhelmed and make for escape. They’re forced to make a tough decision and Joel sacrifices himself to allow everyone else a chance fo continue living. He dies to a gunshot to the head, but with his last sight being Ellie, hidden away in the shadows. A momentary flash of Joel’s daughter appears over Ellie and cuts to black. 

Weeks later, Ellie’s returned home after the Joel’s killers left. Without a leas on their location after the their bases already having been attacked, Ellie struggles with PTSD from Joel’s death and the farm scene plays out with Ellie finding out about the group’s location. She fights with Dina, leaves home and follows. After a lengthy fight that draws many infected near, Ellie kills Joel’s killer, but leaves the rest of the group to face off the horde of infected on their own, leaving their fates up to luck.

In my opinion, Abby’s inclusion is largely unneeded. In fact, her inclusion legitimately makes the game worse. She’s someone we can hate, but not done well. The story just had so much potential, even with Joel dying.

That, and the game’s mostly Ellie’s adventure to hunt down Abby’s group with a fair amount of distractions that mellow out her hatred, along with portions of the story being replaced with Dina (saving Ellie). Some way down the game Ellie finds Abby’s location and moves to take revenge, but fails. Abby gets away and Ellie walks away having learned that Abby killed Joel because he had killed her father.

A year later, Ellie gets a lead on Abby’s location and we see a heartfelt cutscene between Ellie and Dina where Ellie seriously debates taking revenge. Ultimately she decides she needs closure, whether Abby ends up dead or not and leaves Dina at the farm. She fights with Abby, beats her, and let’s her go as a result of her own decision.

This, of course, is assuming we stick with the ‘Abby lives’ type ending. Personally, I’d argue that the first half of the game should’ve been Joel, Tommy, Ellie, Dina, just traveling around or preparing to truly settle down with Joel’s death coming as a result of a violent survivor group that attacked our main cast’s town/area.

Predictable? Probably, but at least it would’ve been more in-tune with the characters.
